clue.text: Plane sailing George's job

parts.note: George is airmen's slang for the automatic ..., so the job George does when a plane is sailing along is steering it

explanation.surface: A description of what someone called George does for a living, apparently plain sailing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plane sailing' plays on the phrase 'plain sailing'; George is RAF slang for the automatic pilot.
explanation.definitionFit: The person or device that steers a plane or guides a ship through harbour does this steering job.

clue.text: Perhaps a chunky sort of hand-grenade?

definitions.text: Perhaps a chunky sort of hand-grenade?

parts.words: Perhaps a chunky sort of hand-grenade?
parts.note: soldiers' slang named the segmented hand-grenade after a tropical fruit, which is also sold tinned in chunks

explanation.surface: A bulky type of explosive.
explanation.walkthrough: The fruit comes tinned in chunks, and its knobbly shape gave the old Mills bomb its slang name.
explanation.definitionFit: The tropical fruit with a scaly rind is sold in chunks and gave its name to grenades of similar shape.

clue.text: She's a lady, Kipling said

parts.note: Rudyard Kipling wrote a poem titled 'The ___ She's a Lady' about a passenger ship

explanation.surface: Kipling vouches for a woman's good breeding.
explanation.walkthrough: Ships are called 'she'; Kipling's poem is 'The Liner She's a Lady'.
explanation.definitionFit: A great passenger ship on a regular route, personified as a lady in Kipling's poem.

clue.text: The betting is he was a tragedian

parts.note: SP is the starting price, the odds offered in betting when a race begins

explanation.surface: A punter reckons an actor was a tragic one.
explanation.walkthrough: SP, the starting price, is the betting odds at the off in British horse racing.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek poet credited as the first actor and inventor of tragedy, whose name gives us thespian.

clue.text: Seaside strip after 11

parts.note: 11 across names a fall in the sea's level; the strip of beach that shows after the tide drops is the one meant

explanation.surface: A stretch of coast described by reference to another clue.
explanation.walkthrough: The cross-reference reads A DROP IN THE OCEAN literally: when the ocean drops at low tide, a strip of seaside is uncovered.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the stretch of beach between high and low water marks, exposed when the tide goes out.

clue.text: Father has these disapproving looks

parts.note: Fr is the abbreviation for Father, a priest's title
to have something is to own it

explanation.surface: Dad gives these stern glances.
explanation.definitionFit: Scowls with a furrowed brow show displeasure.

clue.text: Row about shed damaged by bird

indicators.note: the word row goes about, enclosing the other letters

parts.note: a row is a rank, a line of people or things

indicators.note: something damaged is knocked out of shape, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: An argument over a garden hut wrecked by a bird.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Row' looks like a quarrel, and 'shed' like a garden hut, but row is a line of things and 'damaged' signals the anagram placed inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A wading bird with red legs, common on British coasts and marshes.

clue.text: Mean fellow raised sea-monsters, upsetting my self-esteem

indicators.note: in a down clue, raised means the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: orcs are sea-monsters in old legend, such as the one in Ariosto

indicators.note: upsetting turns the word over in a down clue, writing it upwards

parts.note: ego is one's self-esteem

explanation.surface: A stingy man brings up sea-monsters and knocks my confidence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Raised' turns ORCS to SCRO and 'upsetting' turns EGO to OGE; 'my' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Dickens's miser in A Christmas Carol, whose name now means any stingy person.

clue.text: Bull scored? .No, not on recent form

parts.note: something not on is off

indicators.note: to form something is to shape it anew, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A bull scored at darts, but not in recent form.
explanation.walkthrough: The bull is the bullseye of a dartboard; missing it leaves the dart not quite in the middle. 'Form' turns RECENT into CENTRE.
explanation.definitionFit: A dart that fails to hit the bullseye lands to one side of the middle, slightly misaligned.

clue.text: One is made up, with red dye

indicators.note: made up means put together in a fresh arrangement, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone wears makeup with red dye.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Made up' looks like wearing cosmetics but signals an anagram of ONE IS; 'with' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A red fluorescent dye used to stain biological specimens and in red ink.

clue.text: Unique coinage, not to be repeated

definitions.text: Unique coinage, not to be repeated

parts.words: Unique coinage, not to be repeated
parts.note: coinage here is a newly invented expression, made up for one single occasion only

explanation.surface: A one-off minting of coins that will never be struck again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coinage' suggests money, but it means inventing a word; 'for the nonce' means for this one occasion.
explanation.definitionFit: Lexicographers use this term for an expression invented for a single occasion and not adopted into the language.

clue.text: Birds are' trumps

definitions.meaning: wading birds of the sandpiper family, the males with a showy collar
a verb from card play: plays a trump card on a trick led in another suit

explanation.definitionFit: The noun names sandpiper-like waders; the verb is the bridge and whist term for playing a trump card.

clue.text: Main contribution is negligible

definitions.meaning: the main is poetic for the sea, so this is what one adds to it
an idiom for an amount too small to matter

explanation.definitionFit: Literally a small addition to the sea; idiomatically an amount so tiny compared with the whole that it makes no difference.

clue.text: Fair-minded countrymen borrowed his transport

parts.note: in the folk song about Widecombe Fair, a crowd of Devon villagers borrow one man's grey mare to ride to the fair

explanation.surface: Some honest rustics took a neighbour's vehicle on loan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fair-minded' means minded to go to the fair, not just. In the English folk song 'Widecombe Fair', Tom Pearse lends his grey mare to Uncle Tom Cobley and all.
explanation.definitionFit: Tom of that surname is the owner of the old grey mare in the Devon folk song Widecombe Fair.

clue.text: In this day and age manner of speaking that's become a habit

parts.note: AD, anno Domini, marks the present era
diction is one's manner of speaking

explanation.surface: A modern way of talking that people slip into compulsively.
explanation.walkthrough: AD (Latin anno Domini, in the year of the Lord) dates the present era.
explanation.definitionFit: A compulsive dependence on a drug or practice is a habit in the drug-user's sense.

clue.text: One who takes interest in his surroundings ?

definitions.text: One who takes interest in his surroundings

parts.words: One who takes interest in his surroundings
parts.note: taking interest is earning a return on money put into a business, not showing curiosity about the neighbourhood

explanation.surface: Someone curious about the place around him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Takes interest' is read financially; the question mark hints too at IN VEST, a man inside his undershirt.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who puts capital into shares or a business is rewarded with interest or dividends.

clue.text: The pupils were so astonished!

parts.note: the pupils are the black centres of the eyes, which widen into circles in amazement, not schoolchildren

explanation.surface: A class of schoolchildren gasping in surprise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pupils' suggests a schoolroom, but means the eyes, which go wide in astonishment.
explanation.definitionFit: Wide-eyed with amazement, the eyes opened into circles.

clue.text: Vulgarly a nut-case ?

parts.note: nut is slang for the head, so its case in colloquial speech is the skull

explanation.surface: A rude way of calling someone a lunatic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nut-case' looks like a madman; read as case for the nut (head), it is the skull, informally named.
explanation.definitionFit: A colloquial word for the skull or cranium that holds the grey matter.

clue.text: Aim round fish with a plum-stone perhaps

parts.note: an aim is an end or objective
a round shape is the letter O
carp is a freshwater fish

explanation.surface: Aiming a lure round a fish, with a plum stone as bait.
explanation.definitionFit: Botanists call the hard inner layer of a fruit's wall, such as a plum's stone, by this name.

clue.text: Talk together about one sort of tree

indicators.note: the word for talking together goes about, enclosing the other letter

parts.note: to confer is to talk together
one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: Discussing one particular kind of tree.
explanation.definitionFit: A cone-bearing evergreen such as a pine or fir is a kind of tree.

clue.text: Football money paid to the French takes the cake !

parts.note: the gate is the money taken from spectators at a match
au is French for to the

explanation.surface: Football takings handed over to the French really take the biscuit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Takes the cake' looks like the idiom for something outrageous; here it is a link to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A rich layered French sponge with cream is a type of cake.

clue.text: Hood, say, red or white for a flighty creature

definitions.meaning: Samuel Hood was a famous British naval commander of the eighteenth century

definitions.text: red or white for a flighty creature
definitions.meaning: the red and the white are two British butterflies of the same name

explanation.definitionFit: Lord Hood held the top naval rank; the red and white forms of the name are butterflies.

clue.text: Chesty complication goes with time

indicators.note: a complication tangles things up, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A chest infection gets worse as time passes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chesty complication' suggests bronchitis; 'goes with time' alludes to the Grim Reaper and Father Time, who carry this blade.
explanation.definitionFit: Father Time is pictured carrying the long-bladed mowing tool.

clue.text: The major, perhaps …

parts.note: an army major may be the officer next below the commander of a battalion, the deputy

explanation.surface: An army officer, continued into the next clue's quotation about petty authority.
explanation.walkthrough: The dots run on into 24 across: such a deputy is one 'drest in a little brief authority'.
explanation.definitionFit: A deputy ranking just below the chief officer of a unit, which a major often is in a battalion.

clue.text: I saw the-at Cumae " (Rossetti)

parts.note: a line from Petronius, in Rossetti's translation, about the ancient prophetess of Cumae who longed to die

explanation.surface: A quotation from Rossetti about a sight at Cumae, an ancient Greek colony near Naples.
explanation.walkthrough: Fill in the gap: the Cumaean prophetess of Roman legend, quoted in Rossetti's verse.
explanation.definitionFit: A prophetess of the ancient world, the most famous one living at Cumae.

clue.text: A side on order? That's the truth

parts.note: a cricket or football side is a team of eleven, XI in Roman numerals
the OM is the Order of Merit, a British honour

explanation.surface: A team awaiting instructions, and that is a fact.
explanation.walkthrough: XI is a team of eleven; OM is the Order of Merit; 'on' and 'That's the' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: A self-evident proposition accepted without proof is a basic truth.

clue.text: … "Drest in a little —— authority" (Meas for Meas!)

parts.note: a quotation from Shakespeare's Measure for Measure with one word missing, meaning short-lived

explanation.surface: Isabella's line in Measure for Measure about proud man and his short-lived power.
explanation.walkthrough: Fill in the gap in Shakespeare's 'man, proud man, drest in a little ___ authority'.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's adjective means short in duration, describing authority that lasts only a little while.

clue.text: Acknowledged in a pretty presentation Father's Day

indicators.note: a new presentation of the letters means they are set out in another order

explanation.surface: Being thanked with a pretty gift on Father's Day.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram is of IN A PRETTY, signalled by 'presentation'; 'Acknowledged' and 'on' join it to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Fatherhood, the state of being a parent, is the father's day in the sense of his time or role.

clue.text: Kitchener was not short of such missiles?

definitions.text: Kitchener was not short of such missiles?

parts.words: Kitchener was not short of such missiles?
parts.note: a kitchener was a Victorian cooking stove, a long kitchen range, not the field marshal

explanation.surface: Lord Kitchener, the British field marshal, had plenty of far-reaching weapons.
explanation.walkthrough: Kitchener suggests the First World War commander; a kitchener was also a large iron kitchen range, so it was a long range.
explanation.definitionFit: Missiles that can reach distant targets are described this way, and a big stove is a long cooker.

clue.text: Game, involving a medal

indicators.note: to involve is to roll up or entangle, so the word medal is twisted into a new order

explanation.surface: A sporting contest with a medal at stake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Game' looks like a noun but is the adjective for an injured leg, as in a game leg; 'a' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A game leg is a crippled one, so game here means crippled or disabled.
